case_prompt: A 26-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-week history of fever and painful right-sided neck swelling. She first noted a painful right cervical node, then developed fever up to 40 °C, nausea, and fatigue despite courses of amoxicillin–clavulanate, metronidazole, clindamycin, and naproxen. She had no comorbidities, recent travel, or relevant family history. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable and had three tender enlarged lymph nodes on the right side of her neck; the overlying skin was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10^3/mL, C-reactive protein 77 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/hr, and lactate dehydrogenase 519 U/L. Blood and urine cultures showed no growth, and a tuberculin skin test was negative. Serologic tests demonstrated evidence of past Epstein–Barr virus infection but were negative for HIV, hepatitis B and C, toxoplasmosis, VDRL, ANA, and rheumatoid factor. Chest radiography and CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were unremarkable. Ultrasound and CT of the neck revealed multiple lymph nodes bilaterally extending to the base of the neck and intraparotid region; on the right, posterior-triangle nodes measured up to 18 × 14 mm with rim enhancement and central hypodensity, and on the left, nodes up to 12 × 5 mm appeared reactive. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of an affected lymph node was performed.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Tuberculosis — “tuberculin skin test was also negative.” 2. Viral and other infections (HIV, hepatitis B and C, toxoplasmosis) — “serologic tests for HIV, Hepatitis B and C, toxoplasmosis, venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL), ANA and RF were negative.”

selection.screen_reason: Young woman with fever and tender necrotic cervical nodes unresponsive to antibiotics and a negative infectious and autoimmune workup makes Kikuchi disease the leading answer.
selection.second_look_note: A young woman with fever and tender necrotic cervical nodes unresponsive to several antibiotics and a negative infectious and autoimmune workup makes Kikuchi disease the leading answer.
